name: Cocoa
lede: Cocoa is the brown of cocoa powder, a color name recorded by 1887, for a drink that began in the Americas and was once used as money.

sections.title: The brown of the powder
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary defines cocoa as the brown of cocoa powder and sends the reader on to cacao, the brown of the bean used for making cocoa and chocolate [1]. Cocoa brown, it adds, was a particularly popular color in the 1930s [1]. The same dictionary calls a sienna brown "cocoa colour" [1]. Maerz and Paul (1930) record cocoa as a color name from 1887 [2].

sections.title: A bean before a color
sections.body:
Cocoa beans are native to the Americas [3]. After the Spanish conquest of Mexico, some Spanish settlers took over the local habit of paying with the beans, yet few at first would drink the Aztec chocolate itself [3]. A taste for it grew, helped by sugar, and by the late sixteenth century Spanish owners ran many cocoa plantations in Mexico and Guatemala [3].

Greenfield sets this beside cochineal: cocoa trees fitted a plantation system run on cheap indigenous labor or on enslaved Africans, which the delicate cochineal insect did not [3]. French planters grew cocoa in their Caribbean colonies as well [4]. A colonial council once complained that cochineal-growing commoners were dressing above their station and buying goods once reserved for nobles, the best chocolate among them [3].

sections.title: A cocoa tin
sections.body: The word turns up in a workshop story too. Finlay reports that Redvers-Jones, in a discarded workshop where jet had been worked, found a rusty Cadbury's cocoa tin full of streaks of rouge polish, his clue to the trade name "red devils" [5].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is a moderate yellowish brown, 5 units from ISCC-NBS block 77, and it lies close to [[sandalwood]], [[coffee]] and [[mocha]] [2]. Paterson keeps cocoa, the powder, and cacao, the bean, as separate entries [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Cocoa is a common color in painting. Colors close to it appear in 3,053 of our 23,781 paintings, 12.8 per cent, more than for 94 per cent of the named colors [6]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 34 per cent of the 1,679 paintings where the palette lens finds it [6]. It peaks in the 1200s, in 29 of 142 paintings from then, 2.6 times the museums' baseline [6].

The painter most devoted to it is Hans Smidth, who has it in 8 of his 23 works here, and Tibet is its most over-represented country, in 16 of 47 paintings [6]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not proof of any pigment [6].
